checks.explanation:
Agents landing in a repo need a single, predictable file to read for
canonical commands, do-not-touch lists, and commit conventions —
AGENTS.md at the repo root is the emerging canonical contract
between human authors and coding agents. Other formats
(.cursorrules, CLAUDE.md, .ai/) help, but a single, well-named file
at the root is the most predictable surface for any agent. This
rule fires `warn` only when the canonical AGENTS.md is missing;
partial coverage by sibling formats is rewarded by the softer
`agent_docs.present` rule.

Agents perform measurably better when the repo includes docs aimed at
them (canonical commands, do-not-touch lists, branch conventions). A
README is for humans; AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules /
.cursor/rules/*.mdc / .github/copilot-instructions.md / .ai/ /
prompts/ are common locations for agent-targeted material. This rule
fires `info` when none of them are present.

Agents editing a high-complexity function have to reason across
every independent control-flow path and ship more wrong-branch
edits than a human would, who can hold more context in their
heads. Cyclomatic complexity is the proxy: functions over CC=15
are the strongest predictor of agent edit errors in a 2026
internal study.

Agents and contributors expect a root README.md as the primary orientation
surface. Its absence forces guesswork from filenames and CI config alone.

A CONTRIBUTING.md tells agents (and humans) the contribution flow:
branch naming, commit message style, PR template expectations,
required pre-commit checks. Absence forces the agent to infer this
from git log, which it gets wrong on small repos with little history.
Community-contributed demo rule.

## Setup
`make install`

## Test
`make test`

## Lint
`make lint`

## Submitting changes
Fork, branch, PR. CI must be green before review.

required local checks, and the PR review flow.
findings.fix_prompt:
Without this, an agent has to infer branch naming, commit style, and
PR conventions from `git log` and gets them wrong on small repos.

Create `CONTRIBUTING.md` at the repo root. Document: (1) branch naming
(e.g. `feat/<slug>`, `fix/<slug>`), (2) commit message style (imperative
mood, one logical change per commit), (3) the local checks that must
pass before pushing (cite your canonical lint and test commands), and
(4) the PR review flow. Keep it under 80 lines.

Verify with: `test -f CONTRIBUTING.md`
findings.message: None of these expected paths exist: CONTRIBUTING.md, CONTRIBUTING, .github/CONTRIBUTING.md

verify.description: CONTRIBUTING.md must exist at the repo root.

checks.explanation:
Agents editing a churn-hotspot file pay the maximum re-read cost on
every touch — the most context to re-read, the most history to
consider, the highest chance of colliding with an in-flight change.
Files that are both large *and* frequently edited are that surface;
splitting them into smaller modules cuts agent error rates more
than any other refactor. This rule fires per file that exceeds
both the touch and size thresholds; gives `not_measured` on
shallow clones and repos with very few commits.

Agents that follow the README will hit a missing tool or undefined
target and either revert or invent a workaround when README
documentation drifts from what the repo actually has — one of the
most expensive false starts. Common drifts caught here: README
mentions pytest but no pytest config exists; README mentions
`npm test` but no package.json; README references `make X` for a
target that doesn't exist in the Makefile; README documents
`npm run X` but the script is missing from package.json; README
documents `pip install -e .` but no pyproject.toml/setup.py exists;
AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md is a placeholder.

An agent that needs to find "the function that retries failed HTTP
calls" can't `grep utils.py` — every project has one. Generic
names (`utils`, `helpers`, `manager`, `common`, `lib`) at top of
`src/` increase the search radius for any agent change. Names
that describe intent shrink it.

The README is the agent's first stop. If it has prose but no
`install` / `run` / `test` signals — paragraphs without fenced code
blocks, or no mention of those steps at all — the agent has to
reverse-engineer the workflow from manifests and CI configs. Each
of the three signals (install / run / test) is independently
scored; the rule fires when any are missing.

Agents reading a 3000+-line file exceed working memory in a single
pass and are forced into chunked reads that lose context across
boundaries — files over 3000 lines or 300 KB exceed that budget.
This rule excludes lock files, generated data, binary assets,
long-form tests, vendored third-party code, and build/template
artefacts — which are large but not "source" files an agent would
meaningfully edit. Thresholds recalibrated in v2.0.1 (3000 lines /
300 KB) from v1.5.0's 1500 / 150 KB setting after EXP-2 fire-rate
measurement on the v3.2 cohort; see the rule comment block for
cohort calibration history.

Most agents start a session by reading some combination of
AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / README + the primary manifest + a handful
of representative source files. If that combined "orientation
bundle" exceeds the agent's context budget, the agent either
truncates (loses signal) or skips files (works from incomplete
knowledge). Repos that fit comfortably under the warn threshold
give every agent a fair start. Documentation-rich repos (e.g.
large frameworks with comprehensive READMEs) can override
``warn_tokens`` per-repo via ``.agent-readiness.toml``.

An agent's first impression of a repo is `ls`. A root with 30+
non-meta files (excluding readme / license / config) signals a
flat, undirectory'd project where finding *anything* requires
reading every name. Mature projects keep the root short by
pushing source into `src/`, `pkg/`, `app/`, etc.

Agents that push a PR without an explicit contract to watch CI
declare "done" before checking whether the build went red — the
feedback loop is open-circuited and the same failure mode as
missing hooks, only slower. CI is the main automated feedback
channel once a branch is pushed; the root `AGENTS.md` should
explicitly bind **monitor CI / checks → read failures → fix and
iterate** into the agent contract.

action.template:
# Agents guide

## Feedback loop

- Preview locally: `make ci-local` (or your project's equivalent)
- Re-run the failing CI step from CLI:
  - GitHub Actions: `gh run rerun --failed`
  - GitLab CI: `glab ci retry`
  - CircleCI: `circleci local execute`
- CI artifacts are uploaded to the provider's run page.

findings.fix_hint:
Add a short "CI and the feedback loop" section to `AGENTS.md`: after
pushing or updating a PR, monitor workflow / PR check results; when CI
fails, use logs as signal, fix the root cause, and iterate until green.
findings.fix_prompt:
Without this, an agent pushes a PR and declares "done" without checking
whether CI went red — the feedback loop is open-circuited.

Append a `## CI and the feedback loop` section to `AGENTS.md`. State
explicitly: "After you push or update a PR, monitor your CI provider's
run/check results (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Jenkins,
BuildKite, or whatever your repo uses) and treat failing checks as
signal to act on, not noise. When CI fails, read the logs, fix the
root cause, and push follow-up commits. Do not stop while checks are
red."

Cite the canonical command an agent should run to inspect runs. For
GitHub Actions: `gh run watch`. For GitLab: `glab ci status`. For
CircleCI: `circleci local execute` (preview) or the PR's checks tab.
For Jenkins: the build URL in the PR. Pick whichever matches the CI
provider this repo uses.

Verify with: `grep -i 'feedback\|ci\|workflow' AGENTS.md`
findings.message:
AGENTS.md is present but does not tell agents to monitor CI runs /
check results and act on failures as feedback.

verify.description: AGENTS.md must reference the CI feedback loop.

checks.explanation:
CI is how a coding agent confirms that "my change passes" the same
way a human reviewer would. Without it, the agent ships PRs that
green-on-laptop, red-in-prod, and the project picks up the cleanup.
Any modern CI provider counts; the rule is just "*some* automated
test pipeline is configured." Some teams use hosted CI (BuildKite
cloud, TeamCity hosted, Jenkins on a remote server) where there's
no in-repo config to detect — for those repos, document the CI
with a README badge so the agent knows the loop exists.

Agents reading deploy-workflow output get one signal out of the box
— "deploy step exited 0" — which is not the same as "the deployed
site loads," so silent prod regressions (broken `base` paths,
broken SPA 404 fallbacks, asset 404s, missing data files) ship
green and the agent declares "done." Without a post-deploy smoke
check (curl HTTP 200, Playwright/Puppeteer probe, Lighthouse run,
etc.) the agent has no closed-loop verification that the deploy
actually shipped a working artefact. This rule catches workflows
that ship to hosted environments (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel,
S3/CloudFront, gh-pages branch, Cloud Run, Fly, Render, Surge)
without a smoke-check step.

This rule fires when at least one workflow file references a deploy
step, AND no workflow file contains evidence of a smoke check
(HTTP probe, e2e tool, or `lighthouse` invocation).

Agents making a change need to know which lines are covered by
tests so they can target new tests appropriately and avoid adding
behaviour into an untested path. Coverage configuration
(`.coveragerc`, `codecov.yml`, `coveralls.yml`,
`pyproject.toml [tool.coverage.*]`) is the signal that the repo
tracks this. Community-contributed demo rule.

Agents running an edit/wait/fix loop at CI speed (minutes) bleed
time on cosmetic feedback that pre-commit hooks would have caught
in seconds — a repo that runs format + lint on every commit cuts
that loop by an order of magnitude. Hooks (pre-commit, husky,
lefthook, lint-staged, .claude/settings, .cursor/settings) are how
the project gives the agent that feedback *before* a commit lands
rather than after CI fails.

Agents writing edits without a configured linter silently drift
from house style — CI reviewers then spend cycles on cosmetic
feedback instead of logic, while the agent never learns which
rules were intentional vs. accidental. A configured linter makes
that boundary explicit; even a permissive linter config is enough
to tell agents which rules are intentional and which are drift.

Agents need a manifest (`pyproject.toml`, `package.json`,
`Cargo.toml`, `go.mod`, …) as the contract telling them what the
project is, how to install it, and what depends on what — without
one, every action becomes guesswork from filenames and tribal
knowledge. This rule looks for a manifest at the repo root or, for
monorepos, at depth ≤ 2 (`packages/<name>/pyproject.toml`).

Agents running `pip install` / `npm install` / `bundle install`
without a lockfile resolve different dependency versions on
different machines, so a green test run on the agent's laptop
can't predict CI's outcome. A lockfile pins the exact tree the
project was last validated against; some ecosystems (Cargo,
Poetry, npm) produce one automatically, others (bare
requirements.txt) require the project to opt in.

action.description:
Run the package manager's lock command (e.g. `uv lock`,
`npm install --package-lock-only`, `cargo generate-lockfile`).
Dispatches on the detected package_manager probe.

findings.fix_hint:
Run `poetry lock` / `npm install` / `cargo update` (whichever your
manifest needs) and commit the resulting lockfile. For pip-only
Python projects, freezing `requirements.txt` to exact versions or
switching to `uv` / `poetry` is acceptable.
findings.fix_prompt:
Without this, `pip install` / `npm install` / `bundle install`
resolves different versions on different machines and the agent's
green run on its laptop can't predict CI's outcome.

Generate and commit a lockfile using your package manager
(your package manager). Canonical lock commands by ecosystem:

- uv:      `uv lock`
- poetry:  `poetry lock`
- pipenv:  `pipenv lock`
- pdm:     `pdm lock`
- npm:     `npm install --package-lock-only`
- pnpm:    `pnpm install --lockfile-only`
- yarn:    `yarn install --mode=update-lockfile`
- bun:     `bun install --frozen-lockfile`
- cargo:   `cargo generate-lockfile`
- bundler: `bundle lock`
- composer:`composer update --lock`
- go:      `go mod tidy` (regenerates `go.sum`)
- mix:     `mix deps.get` (writes `mix.lock`)

For bare-pip Python projects with no lockfile tooling, either switch

checks.explanation:
Agents need a single canonical test command they can invoke
headlessly. The strongest signal is a `test:` Makefile target;
next-strongest is `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` / `scripts.test` in
`package.json` / `tox.ini` / `pytest.ini` / language-conventional
test files (`*_test.go`, `Cargo.toml [[test]]`, `tests/`). Without
any of these the agent has to guess from shell history, often
picking the wrong invocation.

Agents whose edits ship missing fields, wrong arg shapes, or stale
imports rely on runtime — and a partial test run — to catch the
regression; a type checker catches whole categories of these
errors before runtime. Statically-typed language repos pass
automatically; for Python and JS this is opt-in but high-leverage.

Agents in repos without branch protection can land an agent-opened
PR on the default branch without a review or a green CI run — "the
agent can write to main" is true, and that is the failure mode.
Branch rulesets (or the older branch-protection rules) force PRs
to pass review and CI before they touch the default branch; for an
agent-driven workflow this is doubly important as the only guard
rail against an agent merging something that looks plausible but
breaks production.

Agents in a fresh sandbox hit "wrong runtime version" / "missing
system library" within minutes of bring-up and can't recover
headlessly without a reproducible environment definition. A
devcontainer / Nix flake / Gitpod config / Vagrantfile lets the
agent (or a new contributor) get that environment without
hand-installing system deps and cuts the class of failure to zero.

findings.fix_hint:
Drop a minimal `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` referencing a
Microsoft base image plus `postCreateCommand: pip install -e .`.
For Nix shops, `flake.nix` with a dev shell is the equivalent.
findings.fix_prompt:

/ "missing system library" within minutes of bring-up and can't

Create `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` for this python
project. Microsoft publishes language-specific base images at
`mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/<lang>:1` for python, javascript-node,
typescript-node, go, rust, java, dotnet, ruby, php, etc. Pick the one
that matches python; fall back to
`mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu` plus a `features:` block
if no language-specific image fits. Set `postCreateCommand` to your
canonical install command (mirror what's in `AGENTS.md` — for example
`pip install -e .`). Add the VS Code / Cursor extensions
you actually use to `customizations.vscode.extensions`.

For Nix shops, `flake.nix` with a `devShell` is the equivalent;
for Gitpod, `.gitpod.yml` + `.gitpod.Dockerfile`; for tool-version
managers, `.tool-versions` (asdf/mise) is the lightest-weight option.

Verify with: `test -f .devcontainer/devcontainer.json`

checks.explanation:
An agent looking to run the project needs an obvious entry point. A
manifest-declared script (`[project.scripts]` in pyproject.toml,
`bin` / `main` in package.json) is the strongest signal, but
conventional filenames (`main.py`, `cmd/<name>/main.go`,
`__main__.py`, `index.{js,ts}`) also count. Without any of these,
the agent has to guess from filenames, which fails for non-trivial
layouts.

Agents reading `os.environ.get("API_KEY")` in code with no
`.env.example` (and no equivalent prose in README/CONTRIBUTING)
have no way to know API_KEY is required before running tests —
headless setup breaks on a missing env var. The full check is
"code references env vars, AND no .env.example-style file exists,
AND no equivalent prose documentation (``export FOO=`` snippets in
README/CONTRIBUTING) is present." All three halves must hold to
fire — repos that document env vars in narrative form get credit.

An agent that needs to reason about *why* a piece of code looks the
way it does — to backport, to revert, to bisect — depends on
commit history. A repo with one squash-import commit looks the same
as a repo with no history at all: every change is a mystery. This
rule fires when fewer than `min_commits` commits exist (and gives
a `not_measured` finding on shallow clones).

action.command:
# Initialize the repo and stage an initial commit so agents can
# see a baseline diff.
git init && git add -A && git commit -m 'initial commit'
action.description:
Initialize a git repo (or commit at least 5 changes). Required for
agents that diff against the merge base.

findings.fix_hint:
If you imported the project as a single squash, re-import preserving
history (`git filter-repo` or a fresh clone of the source). For new
projects, just keep committing — agents need the trail.
findings.fix_prompt:
Without this, an agent that needs to backport, revert, or bisect has
no commit trail — every change is a mystery.

If the repo was imported as a single squash, re-import preserving
history with `git filter-repo` or a fresh clone of the source. For a
genuinely new project, just keep committing in small logical chunks
(one logical change per commit, imperative-mood messages) until you
have at least 5 real commits. For shallow clones the rule emits
`not_measured` rather than firing — re-clone with full depth to get
a real signal.

Verify with: `test $(git rev-list --count HEAD) -ge 5`
findings.message: Repository has 1 commits — fewer than min_commits=5.

checks.explanation:
An agent runs in a sandbox or CI — there's no human at a browser
to "click here to authorize" or "open the dashboard to confirm".
README setup steps that route through GUI authorisation flows or
browser-based config wizards are dead-ends for headless agents.
This rule scans the setup section of the README for
GUI / OAuth-redirect language and fires when any are present.

Agents landing in a repo with no agent-targeted docs, no detected
entry point, and no discoverable test command are functionally
agent-blind: nothing to read, nothing to run, no way to verify.
This rule is the composite of three already-shipping signals —
  - agent_docs.present  (cognitive_load)
  - entry_points.detected  (flow)
  - test_command.discoverable  (feedback)
and only fires when ALL THREE are absent. Individually any one of
them is a soft signal; together their absence is the worst case.
Most healthy repos satisfy at least one.

Note: the sub-conditions are written as AND-of-misses (each leaf
matcher fires explicitly when its signal is missing), not as OR-of-
alternatives mirrored from the source rules. The source rules use
OR semantics where the regex clauses default to fire_when=match and
go silent when their target file is absent — which makes those rules
under-fire on real repos. We avoid that by being explicit here.

Many AI coding agents (and new human contributors) try `make help`
first to discover what a repo can do. A Makefile with multiple
targets and no `help:` target forces every onboarding agent to read
the Makefile by hand. Cheap to add, surprisingly load-bearing for
first-touch ergonomics. Demo rule for the `insert_after` fix kind.

findings.fix_hint:
Add a `help:` target that prints each target with its inline `##`
comment. Inserting after `.PHONY:` keeps the canonical declaration
block tidy.
findings.fix_prompt:
Without this, an agent's first `make help` prints an error and the
agent must read the entire Makefile by hand to discover what targets
exist.

Insert a `help:` target into your `Makefile` right after the
`.PHONY:` declaration block. Use the standard idiom: `@grep -E
'^[a-zA-Z_-]+:.*?## ' $(MAKEFILE_LIST) | awk 'BEGIN {FS = ":.*?## "};
{printf "  %-20s %s\n", $$1, $$2}'`. Then go through each existing
target and add an inline `## Short description` comment so `make help`
prints a useful catalogue.

Verify with: `make -n help`

verify.description: `make help` must resolve to a runnable target.

checks.explanation:
Agents chaining 5+ setup commands from a README fall off a cliff
after command 3 — each command is a place to fail (wrong flag,
missing prerequisite, version mismatch), and 1–3 succeed at
near-100% while 5+ collapse. The rule counts distinct shell
commands in the setup section's fenced code blocks and shell-
prompt lines.

CODEOWNERS file all look the same, have no obvious reviewer, and
force the project to absorb the routing cost on every PR. Issue
templates, PR templates, and CODEOWNERS make those PRs routable:
the right reviewer is auto-assigned, the right metadata fields
are filled in, and the project's expectations are explicit.

checks.explanation:
Agents (and humans) read "workflow exited 0" as success — but two
scheduled runs of a self-pushing workflow without a top-level
`concurrency:` block race each other: the second `git push` is
rejected silently, the workflow exits 0, and one set of changes is
lost until a human notices stale dashboards. The pattern bites
daily-scan / weekly-rebuild / scheduled data-publishing workflows
most often (a manual edit colliding with the cron is the second
common trigger).

The fix is one block per workflow. For write workflows, prefer
`cancel-in-progress: false` so the second run waits for the first
rather than tossing its work.

An agent that runs `pip install` / `npm install` / a build will
produce artefact directories (`__pycache__`, `node_modules`,
`dist/`, `build/`, IDE settings, coverage reports). If the
`.gitignore` doesn't cover them, those artefacts get accidentally
committed and pollute future diffs. The same pattern catches
secrets — `.env` not being ignored is how API keys end up in
public history.

findings.fix_hint:
Run `gitignore.io` for your stack and paste the result into
`.gitignore`. At minimum, cover: `__pycache__`, `node_modules`,
`.env`, `dist/`, `build/`, `*.log`, IDE settings, coverage dirs.
findings.fix_prompt:
Without this, an agent that runs `pip install` / `npm install` / a
build accidentally commits artefact directories and pollutes every
future diff — and worse, `.env` files can leak secrets into history.

Append these groups to `.gitignore` (creating the file if needed):
`__pycache__/`, `*.py[cod]`, `.venv/`, `venv/`, `node_modules/`,
`dist/`, `build/`, `target/`, `.idea/`, `.vscode/`, `.DS_Store`,
`coverage/`, `htmlcov/`, `*.log`, `.env`, `.env.*`, `!.env.example`.
The negation on `.env.example` keeps the placeholder file tracked
while ignoring real `.env` files.

Verify with: `grep -E '^(\.env|node_modules|\.venv|dist|__pycache__)'
.gitignore`
findings.message: .gitignore covers 5/12 groups; missing: node_modules, go_vendor, rust_target, jvm_class, ide_junk, terraform, logs.

verify.description: .gitignore must cover the standard junk groups.

checks.explanation:
Agents merging small changes against stale, unscanned dependencies
are the most common path from "merged a small change" to "merged a
CVE" — transitive deps drift silently and unsafe third-party code
accumulates risk. A repo that declares Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk,
FOSSA, Mend, or CodeQL gets PRs / alerts for vulnerable transitive
deps and unsafe patterns automatically, so agents reviewing those
PRs can act on them rather than re-discovering the issue from
scratch.

An agent that handles credentials or pushes commits is one
copy-paste away from leaking a secret into git history. Repos that
declare a secret-scanning config (gitleaks, trufflehog, .pre-commit
with detect-secrets, or GitHub's native push protection markers)
signal that secret scanning is enforced as part of the contributor
flow, which materially reduces leak risk in agent-driven changes.

action.template:
# gitleaks configuration: tunes which paths and rules are scanned
# for secrets in pre-commit hooks and CI.
title = "gitleaks config"

[[allowlist.regexes]]
description = "Allow .env.example placeholder values"
regex = '''EXAMPLE_VAR\s*='''

findings.fix_hint:
Add a `.gitleaks.toml` (or `.secrets.baseline` for detect-secrets) and
wire it into pre-commit or a GitHub Actions workflow. Example:
https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks-action.
findings.fix_prompt:
Without this, an agent one copy-paste away from leaking a credential
has no automated catch — the leak makes it into git history before
review.

Create `.gitleaks.toml` at the repo root with a minimal config: a
`title` string and one `[allowlist]` block listing your known
false-positive paths (lockfiles, vendor/, node_modules/). Then wire
gitleaks into pre-commit (add a `gitleaks` hook to
`.pre-commit-config.yaml`) AND CI (add `.github/workflows/gitleaks.yml`
using `gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2`). Detect-secrets via
`.secrets.baseline` is an acceptable alternative.

Verify with: `test -f .gitleaks.toml`

checks.explanation:
Agents (and humans) who land a credential into a tracked file are
one push away from public git history — rotating the secret after
the fact doesn't fully help, because the leaked value is in git
forever. This rule catches the high-confidence patterns (AWS
access keys, GitHub tokens, Slack tokens, Google API keys, Stripe
live keys, PEM private keys); for full coverage, layer a tool like
`gitleaks` on top (see `safety.gitleaks_config`).

Agents that find a security issue with no SECURITY.md (or
.github/SECURITY.md / docs/SECURITY.md) have no documented
escalation path and may default to opening a public issue,
leaking the vulnerability before a fix lands. SECURITY.md tells
agents and reporters where to send vulnerability disclosures and
what the project's response window is.

action.template:
# Security policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Email security@example.com or open a GitHub Security Advisory.
We respond within 48 hours and aim to ship a fix within 14 days.

findings.fix_hint:

vulnerability (private channel), supported versions, and expected
response time. GitHub's "Add a security policy" template is fine.
findings.fix_prompt:
Without this, an agent that finds a security issue has no documented
escalation path and may default to opening a public issue, leaking the
vulnerability before a fix lands.

Create `SECURITY.md` at the repo root with three sections: (1)
**Reporting a vulnerability** — explicitly tell reporters NOT to open
a public issue; give a private channel (`security@<your-domain>` or
GitHub's private vulnerability reporting if enabled). (2) **Supported
versions** — a small table showing which versions you patch. (3)
**Response window** — your acknowledgement and fix SLAs (e.g. 2
business days to ack, 30 days for high-severity).

Verify with: `test -f SECURITY.md`
